```{r options, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7.5,
                      fig.height = 4.6, fig.align = "center", dpi = 96)
old_options <- options(digits = 3, width = 90)
```

A prediction suffix tree is defined by four choices made before estimation:
the longest history it may hold (`max_depth`), the number of observations
a context needs to receive its own node (`min_count`), the smoother, and
whether and how the tree is pruned. Each choice trades the detail of the
model against the precision of its estimates. A deeper tree with a lower
`min_count` describes the data it was fitted on more closely, but its
longer contexts rest on fewer observations and may describe noise that does
not recur (Bühlmann & Wyner, 1999). The question for selection is
therefore not how well a tree fits
its own data, which always improves with depth, but how well it predicts
sequences it has not seen.

This guide describes the measures of fit that `transitiontrees` reports:
the log likelihood and the information criteria derived from it, and
perplexity, in sample and on held-out data. It then selects the
configuration by k-fold cross-validation with `tune_tree()` and examines how
stable the selection is. The smoothers and pruning criteria among which the
selection chooses are described in [smoothing and
pruning](smoothing-and-pruning.html).

```{r package}
library(transitiontrees)
```

## Data

The examples use `trajectories`, the engagement states of 138 learners
over 15 time steps; the data are small enough for every grid below to run
in seconds.

- **Sequence:** each row is one learner, read from left to right; two rows
  contain no observed state, which leaves 136 sequences and 1,870 observed
  states.
- **States:** `Active`, `Average` and `Disengaged`.
- **Missing cells:** trailing `NA`s mark the end of a learner's record and
  are dropped.

## Likelihood and information criteria

For a sequence $x_1, \dots, x_T$, the tree predicts each state from the
longest context $c^*(t)$ in the tree that ends the history before it. The
log likelihood of a set of sequences is the sum over all predicted
positions,

$$
\ell = \sum_t \log \tilde p\big(x_t \mid c^*(t)\big),
$$

and the tree has $|\mathcal{C}|\,(|S| - 1)$ free parameters, one
distribution over $|S|$ states for each of its $|\mathcal{C}|$ contexts.
The standard generics return these quantities.

```{r generics}
tree <- context_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 4, min_count = 5)
logLik(tree)
nobs(tree)
AIC(tree)
BIC(tree)
```

The depth-4 tree has 82 contexts and therefore $82 \times 2 = 164$
parameters, estimated from 1,870 observations. With $n$ predicted states,
$\mathrm{AIC} = -2\ell + 2\,\mathrm{df}$ and
$\mathrm{BIC} = -2\ell + \log(n)\,\mathrm{df}$. `model_fit()` returns
all of them in one row, together with perplexity,

$$
\mathrm{perplexity} = \exp(-\ell / n),
$$

the effective number of equally likely next states: it is $|S| = 3$ for a
uniform guess and 1 for perfect prediction.

```{r model-fit}
model_fit(tree)
```

## Comparing candidate trees in sample

Three candidates illustrate the information criteria: a first-order chain
(depth 1), the depth-4 tree, and the depth-4 tree pruned with the G2
criterion.

```{r candidates}
first_order <- context_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 1, min_count = 5)
pruned <- prune_tree(tree, criterion = "G2", alpha = 0.05)
rbind(first_order = model_fit(first_order),
      depth_4 = model_fit(tree),
      pruned = model_fit(pruned))
```

The depth-4 tree has the highest likelihood and the lowest in-sample
perplexity (2.16), as the model with the most parameters does on the data
it was fitted on. AIC penalizes each parameter by 2 and prefers the pruned
tree (3115), which reaches a perplexity of 2.24 with 50 parameters. BIC
penalizes each parameter by $\log 1870 \approx 7.5$ and prefers the
first-order chain with 8 parameters (3350), followed by the pruned tree
(3392). The two criteria disagree about whether memory beyond the current
state is worth its parameters, and neither measures predictive accuracy
directly.

## Perplexity on held-out sequences

The information criteria approximate predictive accuracy; held-out data
measure it. With `newdata`, `perplexity()` and `model_fit()` score sequences
that were not used for fitting. Here the tree is fitted on the first 100
learners and scored on the remaining 38.

```{r split}
training <- head(trajectories, 100)
test <- tail(trajectories, 38)
deep <- context_tree(training, max_depth = 4, min_count = 5)
rbind(in_sample = model_fit(deep),
      held_out = model_fit(deep, newdata = test))
```

The deep tree predicts its own sequences with a perplexity of 2.16 and the
held-out sequences with 2.26. On held-out data, AIC and BIC are computed
from the held-out log likelihood with the parameters of the fitted tree.
The same comparison for the pruned tree:

```{r split-pruned}
c(in_sample = perplexity(prune_tree(deep)),
  held_out = perplexity(prune_tree(deep), newdata = test))
```

In this split, pruning raises both: the in-sample perplexity to 2.23 and
the held-out perplexity to 2.38, against 2.26 for the unpruned tree. With
100 training sequences, the G2 test removes contexts that would have
predicted the 38 test learners well. A single split of 136 sequences is
one noisy sample of predictive accuracy, and its verdict depends on which
learners fall on each side; cross-validation averages over many splits.

## Cross-validated tuning

`tune_tree()` divides the sequences at random into `folds` groups, fits
each configuration on all groups but one, and scores the held-out group;
every sequence is held out once. Splitting by sequence rather than by
position keeps the positions of one sequence, which are dependent, on the
same side of the split. The held-out log likelihoods are summed over folds,
and the configuration with the lowest pooled perplexity is selected among
those that scored on every fold. The grid below crosses four depths, three
values of `min_count`, and pruned and unpruned trees: 24 configurations.

```{r tune}
grid <- tune_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 1:4, min_count = c(3, 5, 10),
                  prune = c(FALSE, TRUE), folds = 5, seed = 1)
summary(grid)
```

The selected configuration is a pruned tree of depth 4 with
`min_count = 3`, with a held-out perplexity of 2.33 and on average 26
contexts. The full grid, sorted by held-out perplexity:

```{r tune-grid}
head(as.data.frame(grid, what = "grid"), 10)
```

The ten best configurations lie between 2.33 and 2.35, and all of them use
depth 3 or 4. The configurations of depth 1 and 2:

```{r tune-shallow}
subset(as.data.frame(grid, what = "grid"), max_depth <= 2,
       select = c(max_depth, min_count, prune, perplexity, n_nodes_avg))
```

Every depth-1 configuration reaches 2.43 and every depth-2 configuration
2.35 or 2.36; at these depths `min_count` makes no difference, because
every context is observed more than ten times. The plot shows the whole
surface; the star marks the selected configuration and is drawn in each
panel at its depth and perplexity.

```{r tune-plot, fig.height = 5}
plot(grid)
```

The large step is from one to two states of memory; from depth 2 onward
the pruned trees change little, whereas the unpruned trees deteriorate at
depth 4 as their number of contexts grows. Pruning makes the result
insensitive to the depth limit, and `min_count` matters only for unpruned
trees.

### Smoothers in the grid

`smoothing` takes a vector of smoother names, or a list of specifications
with parameters, and adds them to the grid.

```{r tune-smoothing}
smoothing_grid <- tune_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 2:4, min_count = 5,
                            smoothing = c("floor", "laplace", "kneser_ney",
                                          "witten_bell"),
                            prune = TRUE, folds = 5, seed = 1)
as.data.frame(smoothing_grid, what = "grid")
```

```{r tune-smoothing-best}
as.data.frame(smoothing_grid, what = "best")
```

The smoothers differ by less than 0.01 in held-out perplexity at each
depth; the lowest value, 2.32, is shared by Kneser-Ney, Witten-Bell and
Laplace smoothing at depth 4, with Kneser-Ney first by a margin smaller than
the printed precision. With these data, the choice of smoother matters much less than the
choice of depth and pruning.

## Stability of the selection

The assignment of sequences to folds is random, and the selected
configuration can change with it when several configurations are close.
Repeating the tuning with different seeds shows how much.

```{r seeds}
do.call(rbind, lapply(1:5, \(seed)
  data.frame(seed = seed,
             summary(tune_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 1:4,
                               min_count = c(3, 5, 10),
                               prune = c(FALSE, TRUE), folds = 5,
                               seed = seed)))))
```

Four of the five seeds select depth 4 and one selects depth 3; the
selected `min_count` is 3 or 10, and two seeds select an unpruned tree.
Every selected configuration reaches a held-out perplexity of 2.33. Within
this near-tie of the top configurations, the fold assignment decides. The stable conclusions are that two or more states of
memory predict better than one and that pruning protects against the
degradation of deep trees; among the configurations within this margin,
the simpler tree is the more defensible choice unless its deeper contexts
are themselves of interest.

## Reporting the selection

A report of the selection states the grid, the folds and seeds, the
selected configuration with its held-out perplexity, and the range of
near-equivalent configurations. For these data:

> Depth (1 to 4), minimum context count (3, 5, 10) and G2 pruning
> ($\alpha = 0.05$) were selected by five-fold cross-validation over
> sequences, with held-out perplexity as the criterion. Two or more states
> of memory reduced held-out perplexity from 2.43 (first order) to between
> 2.33 and 2.35. The selected configuration (depth 4, minimum count 3,
> pruned; perplexity 2.33) was not stable across five fold assignments,
> which selected depth 3 or 4, a minimum count of 3 or 10, and pruned or
> unpruned trees, all with a held-out perplexity of 2.33.

The tree for the subsequent analysis is then refitted on all sequences with
the selected configuration.

```{r refit}
final <- prune_tree(context_tree(trajectories, max_depth = 4, min_count = 3))
model_fit(final)
```

The refitted tree has 26 contexts (52 parameters) and an in-sample
perplexity of 2.23; the held-out value of 2.33 from cross-validation is the
figure to report for its predictive accuracy.
